title: A House for the Well
premise: Orsen Ashgrove, a pest controller who copes with a fractured childhood by documenting everything, is called to Hollowell House to deal with 'something with fingerprints' — handprints appearing in dust, flour, and ash that belong to no living resident. On the porch waits Wick, the imaginary friend Orsen invented at age seven, unchanged after thirty years, and the house begins rewriting Orsen's memories to make room for them both. Digging into the house's history, Orsen learns that in 1974 the previous family's youngest son vanished, taken by the house as a 'found child' to replace the one it lost — and that Wick is that boy, worn down into something imaginary by decades of being forgotten. To free Wick and themselves, Orsen must return the boy's true name and remains to his grieving, still-living sister, breaking the house's claim before it finishes rewriting Orsen out of existence; the house collapses into the well at its heart, and Orsen, no longer invisible, chooses the found family that finally sees them.
about_author: Freya Quintana is the pen name of a former archival assistant who spent six years cataloguing estate sales and unclaimed property, an experience that taught her how objects remember. She writes horror about the tenderness that survives inside haunted places and lives in a drafty farmhouse she insists is only a house.

chapters.title: The Call Sheet
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A routine pest-control call to Hollowell House turns strange: the client describes 'something with fingerprints,' and Orsen, who documents everything as a form of prayer, begins their log. The emotional beat is wary competence masking loneliness — Orsen takes jobs no one else wants because being needed is the closest thing to belonging they have.

chapters.title: Handprints in the Flour
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Small handprints appear in the kitchen flour overnight, sized for a child of about seven, always facing outward, as if waving goodbye. The current owner, Mara, admits the house came furnished with its history — and its silences. Orsen photographs, measures, logs. The beat: the comfort of procedure beginning to crack against evidence of something patient.

chapters.title: The Porch
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Leaving at dusk, Orsen finds a figure on the porch steps: Wick, the imaginary friend from their seventh year, unchanged, waving exactly as the handprints did. Orsen's documentation instinct fails for the first time — no camera will hold Wick's image. The beat is terror braided with a shameful, aching joy at being remembered.

chapters.title: What Documentation Cannot Hold
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, interleaved with log entries that contradict each other. Orsen tests Wick: dates, names, childhood facts — Wick knows things Orsen never told anyone, and some things Orsen never knew at all. The beat: identity destabilizing, as Orsen wonders whether they invented Wick or Wick invented them.

chapters.title: The House That Keeps Children
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara reveals the house's reputation: children who lived here describe a 'third sibling' no adult could see, in every generation since 1951. She's staying because leaving feels impossible — the house gets 'sad' when they pack. The beat: dawning complicity; Mara is a keeper who never chose the job.

Orsen's POV at the county archive. Records show the Halloway family: three children, then two, after the youngest, Edmund, vanished in October 1974. The case file is thin — but a neighbor's statement mentions Edmund 'playing with a friend only he could see.' The beat: the horror clicking into focus; Orsen recognizes the shape of the story because it is their own.

chapters.title: Wick's Version
chapters.summary: Wick's POV, the first chapter from inside the house's logic. Wick remembers the well, the game they played, the promise Edmund made — and the slow erosion of being forgotten, name dissolving into 'Wick,' a candle-stub of a boy kept lit by one child's attention at a time. The beat: heartbreaking sympathy; the monster is a lonely child who never got to stop being one.

chapters.title: The Well Room
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen finds a door behind the pantry that wasn't there before, opening onto a room with an old stone well at its center — dry, but echoing. Handprints ring the rim, hundreds, generations deep. The beat: the house showing itself; documentation becomes useless as the room rearranges between photographs.

chapters.title: Rewritten
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen's own memories begin editing: their childhood home feels wrong, their mother's face blurs, and a new memory of Hollowell House as 'home' keeps trying to settle in. They fight back the only way they know — writing everything down, verbatim, hourly. The beat: desperate resistance; the log becomes a lifeline and a countdown.

chapters.title: Mara's Confession
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara admits she has seen the third sibling too, as a child in this house, and let him go — and the house punished her with thirty years of dreams. She begs Orsen to leave before it finishes 'keeping' them. The beat: guilt and warning; two keepers, one generation apart, finally speaking.

chapters.title: The Sister
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV on the road. Orsen locates Edmund's sister, Ruth Halloway, now in her sixties, who has never believed her brother ran away. She gives Orsen a shoebox: Edmund's baby teeth, a name bracelet, a letter he wrote the week he vanished. The beat: fragile hope; the tools of return exist, if Orsen can carry them back.

chapters.title: Names Have Weight
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Back at the house, Orsen speaks Edmund's name aloud and the whole structure shudders; Wick appears, flickering, half-remembering himself. The house retaliates — doors relocate, the well room moves deeper, and Orsen's log pages begin blanking. The beat: escalation; naming is power, and the house knows it.

chapters.title: The House's Hunger
chapters.summary: Wick's POV. The house, given voice through Wick's fading mind, reveals its logic: it lost its own child to the well in 1951 and has been 'finding' replacements ever since, wearing them down into imaginary friends when they resist. Orsen is the first keeper strong enough to matter. The beat: the antagonist's tragic, monstrous motive laid bare.

chapters.title: What Orsen Was Running From
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Forced into the well room, Orsen confronts the memory the house has been using: the childhood neglect that made an imaginary friend necessary, the years of feeling invisible. The house offers a bargain — stay, be kept, be loved, forever. The beat: the thematic crucible; belonging offered as captivity.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen refuses — not because the love is fake, but because being kept isn't being seen. They declare, in the log, in the room, aloud: 'I am not your found child.' The house begins taking them anyway, and Wick, flickering at the rim of the well, makes a choice of his own. The beat: defiant clarity at the cost of safety.

chapters.title: Wick Remembers
chapters.summary: Wick's POV. Orsen's refusal gives Wick strength to reclaim his name: Edmund. In a surge of recovered memory he shows Orsen where his remains were hidden — not in the well, but beneath its dry stones, wrapped in the coat his mother sewed. The beat: identity reclaimed; the imaginary friend becomes a real boy with a real grave.

chapters.title: Digging
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, Mara assisting. In the collapsing well room, they dig by candlelight while the house screams through the plumbing and the walls grow handprints by the dozen, all facing inward now. The beat: frantic, physical climax-building; the house fighting for its child with everything it has.

chapters.title: The Return
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. They lift out the small bundle, and the house goes utterly silent — the silence of held breath. Orsen speaks the return: Edmund Halloway, born 1966, taken 1974, found. Wick/Edmund begins to solidify, aging years in seconds. The beat: sacred dread; the prayer of documentation finally answered.

chapters.title: The Well Takes It Back
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The house demands a replacement — the bargain was never optional, it claims. Edmund steps toward the well himself, offering to stay, and Orsen stops him: 'You were never the house's. You were hers.' They carry him out together as the structure tears itself apart around them. The beat: climax; found family literally carrying each other out of the dark.

chapters.title: Ruth
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. At her kitchen table, Orsen gives Ruth the shoebox and the truth, and Ruth embraces a brother who is thirty years too old and exactly the right age. Grief and joy in the same breath. The beat: catharsis; the return is complete — not to the house, but to the living.

chapters.title: The Last Log Entry
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Hollowell House stands empty and ordinary, its well room a plain cellar, its handprints gone. Mara stays — by choice now, as its caretaker, not its keeper. Orsen closes the log, then opens a new notebook: not documentation, but a letter to their mother. The beat: quiet resolution; the archive becomes outreach.

chapters.title: A House for the Well
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, one year later. Orsen visits Ruth and Edmund on Sundays, has a key to Mara's house, and is teaching a young apprentice who calls them 'found family' without irony. On the porch of their own small house, for one second, a handprint waves in the dust — and Orsen, unafraid, waves back. The beat: belonging chosen, not kept; the horror transmuted into grace.
